body:
this input program:

```c
int f( int)
{
    return 0 ;
}

int a;
static int b = f ( a) ;
````
options:
`/T ps_6_2 /E f`

causes
either:

> Internal compiler error: access violation. Attempted to read from address 0x0000000000000018

either:
> error: llvm::cast<X>() argument of incompatible type!

randomly.

_dxc versions tested: 1.6.x and 1.7.2212.12_

comments.body:
Hi, thanks for the report!

This can be reproduces at head (ce9b3a2c8b56d9e24b5f3cdfa24c8c938eafb56e), and yields the following error:

```
otherwise we flattened a library function.dxc: lib/Transforms/Scalar/ScalarReplAggregatesHLSL.cpp:6093: void (anonymous namespace)::SROA_Parameter_HLSL::replaceCall(llvm::Function *, llvm::Function *): Assertion `false && "otherwise we flattened a library function."' failed.
Aborted
```

Just unsure what the given shader as input is supposed to do, since it's building a PS with `f` as entrypoint, but has no semantic and some unused globals. Tried to add a minimal PS main using b, but this works fine.

Can you reproduce this with a "valid" shader?
(Compiler crashing instead of refusing is still something to fix, just want to check if this is for a valid use-case or not)
It is not for a valid use case. It's an attack.

I'm unsure what the point of calling it an attack is... This becomes a recoverable error in the library interface, the standalone compiler reports the error.

It is invalid shader code that we don't produce a good error for.

The standalone compiler crashes, it does not report an error. Therefore in the worst scenario it can potentially be used as 0 day exploit on service sites like Tim Jones playground or godbolt. In that regard, it may be called an attack. In general a crashing input is reasonable to label "attack" in any sort of software, be it malicious or unintended.

The messages you’re reporting are printed by the exception handler. There is no crash. The process terminated and cleans up as expected:

https://github.com/microsoft/DirectXShaderCompiler/blob/main/tools/clang/tools/dxclib/dxc.cpp#L1291

Running this repro shader on the latest release & head on linux doesn't hit the exception handler, but makes an invalid pointer load in GlobalIsNeeded (since assert are disabled) and segv. So it's something that should be fixed at some point.

Now, for the prioritization, it's a compiler, running on an old, fixed version of llvm/clang, so we crash a lot (even upstream has its fair share of unresolved segv (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+segmentation+fault), so imagine us 😊)

We might try to fix this issue depending on bandwidth, I personally don't believe it to be the top-priority vs actual valid shaders that also crash/don't compile (PR welcome 😊)
(As for godbolt/shader-playground, I'd expect them to treat DXC, its input and output as dangerous by default, since it's a compiler)

> Running this repro shader on the latest release & head on linux doesn't hit the exception handler, but makes an invalid pointer load in GlobalIsNeeded (since assert are disabled) and segv. So it's something that should be fixed at some point.

On Windows the memory access issue becomes a SEH which we catch. On Linux, the signal should get handled by the registered signal handler. Are we not registering the signal handler?

Isn't it actually better to leave the program crash in that case?
This is not a normal error, we have a garbage pointer that we try to load. Understanding & debugging seems simpler when we don't catch those.
Is that because you want the lib to return a "internal error" without crashing the host process?

On Windows in SEH, we can continue because the stack unwinds sufficiently.
On *nix, the signal handler should either call `abort()` or `raise()` to terminate execution.

In either case, termination of execution is controlled.
I'm surprised anyone would consider SEH catch as a valid programming practice.

Catching fatal exceptions can be a valid practice, as you can provide the user with a better context to share, allowing better issue reporting:
 - you can print a backtrace
 - you can dump registers info, or do a coredump-like feature.

> I'm surprised anyone would consider SEH catch as a valid programming practice.

Personally I dislike exceptions and would love if we didn’t use exceptions or RTTI in DXC… That’s not my choice to make. DXC uses SEH (whether I like it or not), which means we don’t have an uncontrolled crash for cases like this.
